title: Care for the whole person
hook: Jesuit schools care for the whole person

segments.voice: Yesterday, contemplatives in action: no choir bell, a day built for being sent, and a still point to return to. Your line was prayer in motion. Which errand did it ride along with? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

A report card says a student is failing chemistry. One teacher sees a grade to fix. Another teacher notices the student has been sleeping in the back row for weeks, asks a quiet question after class, and learns that someone at home is sick and the kid is working nights. Same student, same grade. Two very different pictures of who is sitting in that chair. Jesuit schools have a two-word Latin phrase for the second kind of seeing, and some put it in their mission statements. Today's word.
screen: `A FAILING GRADE.` → `A QUIET QUESTION AFTER CLASS.` → `WHO IS IN THAT CHAIR?`

segments.voice: Cura personalis. Cura means care. Personalis means of the person. Care for the person, and in English it usually comes out as care for the whole person. The idea is older than the slogan. When Ignatius wrote the guidance at the start of the Spiritual Exercises, he kept telling the director to adapt. Give the Exercises according to the person's age, education and ability. Don't hand someone more than they can carry. Notice whether they are in consolation or desolation, and respond to that person, not to a script. The retreat bends to fit the human being, not the other way round. Later Jesuits, tradition says, used cura personalis for the care superiors owed each member of the order, one by one. Jesuit schools took it up as a promise about students: we are not only training a mind. We care about the body that's tired, the heart that's worried, the spirit that's searching. Saint Paul's blessing for the Thessalonians names all three, in the Douay-Rheims: "your whole spirit, and soul, and body." Here's what makes it more than kindness. A Jesuit classroom is still a classroom. The chemistry still matters. Cura personalis doesn't lower the bar; it asks who is trying to clear it, and what they're carrying. And it isn't only for schools. A nurse can practice it, a manager, a parent at a kitchen table. It's the difference between how are you, said on the way past, and how are you, said while you stop walking.
screen: `CURA: CARE. PERSONALIS: OF THE PERSON.` · `IGNATIUS: ADAPT TO EACH ONE.` · `MIND, BODY, HEART, SPIRIT.` · `IT DOESN'T LOWER THE BAR.` · then, large: `YOUR WHOLE SPIRIT, AND SOUL, AND BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to ask how someone really is. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you'll see or message today. A coworker, a parent, a friend who's gone quiet. Picture them not as a role, the boss, the roommate, but as a whole person: what might their body be carrying, their mind, their heart? Then choose the moment you'll ask, and plan to stop and wait for the real answer. If you pray, you can hold that person before God for the length of this sit. The bell holds the time.
Cura personalis. Latin for care of the person: the Jesuit habit of attending to each one as a whole human being, mind, body and spirit. Today's word.
Your line: the whole person. Today, ask one person how they really are, then stop walking, and wait. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Jesuit schools and universities describe cura personalis as attention to each student's intellectual, emotional and spiritual life, and the phrase often appears in their mission statements and advising programs.

fork.setup: you're a teacher. a good student starts failing and sleeping in class. what does cura personalis ask of you first?
options: lower the grade standard for them.
ask quietly what's going on, and listen.
report the grade and move on.
fork.reveal: care for the whole person starts by seeing who's in the chair. the standard can stay; the student is no longer just a grade.

original.note: Latin: care of the person. a phrase Jesuit schools use for their care of each student.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line from a school brochure.
what it means: attending to each person as a whole, mind, body, heart and spirit, without lowering the bar.
what a scholar hears: an echo of Ignatius's insistence that the Exercises be adapted to each person, and a phrase Jesuits used for a superior's care of each member.
